| [THEORY-058](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-058.md) v2 | Mental disorders are maintained by self-reinforcing causal loops rather than expressing a latent common cause, which is how they can outlast their triggers | Three traditions that do not cite one another for it put self-sustaining loops where a latent cause would be. Borsboom ([LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md)) makes disorder an alternative stable state of a strongly connected symptom network, kept up by hysteresis after its trigger has gone. Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)) make it a threat meaning protected by the behaviour it drives. Kendler ([LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md)) finds causal loops across levels, from genes to culture. The convergence is real; the evidence is indirect, simulated or clinical, and none of it is an individual time series showing hysteresis, so the account is Proposed. It says nothing about what starts a disorder. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-097](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-097.md) | Long-range coordination in the human forebrain is carried by brief ripples that co-occur at distant sites: during them neurons co-fire more whatever the distance between them, and at retrieval they carry stimulus-specific reinstatement of encoding co-firing | Verzhbinsky, Daume, Cheng, Rutishauser & Halgren (2026), [LIT-633](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-633.md): in 1,373 single units from five bilateral forebrain regions of 35 epilepsy patients doing a Sternberg task, ripples (70–100 Hz, about 70 ms) co-occur between bundles at a median 5% at every tract distance from 71 to 223 mm, and unit pairs co-fire a median 34% more during co-ripples than in no-ripple periods, beyond a rate-only null and with no loss over distance. The gain rises with load (13% in maintenance, 19% at retrieval), and encoding co-firing for a stimulus recurs at retrieval in 0.29% of cell-pair trials in co-ripples against 0.14% outside them. Correlational throughout: one task, two load levels, clinically placed electrodes, nothing perturbed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-143](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-143.md) | When a group learns only about the options its members pursue and good evidence is scarce, sparser communication makes it more likely to settle on the better option, at a large cost in speed; when evidence is plentiful, sparsity only slows learning | Zollman (2007), [LIT-724](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-724.md), simulated Bala and Goyal's bandit model: cycles chose the better method more often than complete graphs, and more slowly; density, not centrality, predicted failure. Rosenstock et al. (2017), [LIT-733](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-733.md), found the effect only where inquiry is hard: close alternatives, small groups, small batches. Proposed: all of it is simulation, and real communities' place in parameter space is unknown. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-146](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-146.md) | Industry can bias a scientific community toward a worse treatment without corrupting any individual, by selectively funding researchers whose methods already favour its product, provided researchers differ in method and both influence and the training of newcomers follow productivity; an independent funder counteracts this only if it discounts industry-funded work, and one that funds on productivity alone makes it worse | Holman & Bruner (2017), [LIT-744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-744.md). In a Zollman bandit model with methodological diversity, productivity-weighted influence and turnover, industry funding of agents whose methods favour the drug lowers the chance of converging on the better action, though no agent's beliefs respond to funding. A merit-based independent funder worsens it; one ignoring industry-funded trials counters it. Proposed: one case and a small simulation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-148](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-148.md) | A group learning by trying needs diversity in what its members pursue that lasts long enough to survive misleading early evidence and then gives way to consensus; limited communication and stubborn priors each supply it, and together they make it permanent, so the group never settles | Zollman (2010), [LIT-735](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-735.md): in a bandit model with beta priors, sparse networks and extreme priors each maintain diversity of pursuit and each improve reliability, but combined they keep diversity alive so long that agents fail to converge. Rosenstock et al. [LIT-733](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-733.md) find this the result that is robust across the models they test. Proposed: shown only in simulation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-178](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-178.md) | Transcriptional regulation alone can make a bacterium's gene-expression state depend on its history: a transient change to one regulator can leave its regulatory network in a different self-maintaining state, but only through a gene that reaches a positive circuit | Zhao, Wytock, Reynolds and Motter (2024), [LIT-854](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-854.md). In an ensemble of sign-consistent Boolean rules on the 87-gene core of the E. coli regulatory network, 51 genes admit a transient knockout or overexpression that moves the network to a different attractor, and every such gene reaches a strongly connected component with a positive circuit. So one genotype may hold several heritable expression states without epigenetic marks. The evidence is a model ensemble; no transient perturbation has been shown to have a lasting effect in cells, so the account is Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-188](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-188.md) | In a random graph whose nodes lie in a hyperbolic disk and connect by distance, a power-law degree distribution and strong clustering follow from the geometry: the degree exponent is set by node density relative to curvature, clustering by a temperature, and removing the angular, metric part of the distance leaves the configuration model | Krioukov, Papadopoulos, Kitsak, Vahdat and Boguñá (2010), [LIT-865](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-865.md): derived, in a large-distance approximation, for a model in the hyperbolic plane, with simulations. γ = 2α/ζ + 1; clustering falls from its maximum at T = 0 to zero at a transition at T = 1; a circle model with power-law hidden degrees is the same ensemble once degree is radial depth; dropping the angular term gives the configuration model. It does not show that any real network is hyperbolic, or that hierarchy causes heterogeneity. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md) | The S¹ hidden-metric network model is approximately closed under geometric coarse-graining: merging angular neighbours keeps its connection law with β fixed, and the average degree flows as r^ν with ν set by the degree exponent and β | García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md): derived to first order, checked on one synthetic network over eight layers and on six real ones. Supernode hidden degree is the ℓ^β sum of its members'; β is invariant; ⟨k⟩ scales by r^ν with ν = 2/(γ−1) − 1 or 2/β − 1, flowing to a complete graph if γ < 3 or β < 2 and to a ring if γ > 3 and β > 2. It does not show that real networks are generated by a hidden metric space, or that the nested layers are a hierarchy found in the data. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-193](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-193.md) | A simplicial complex grown by gluing each new d-simplex to one (d − 1)-face, by a rule that uses no geometry, has a tree as its dual and, with every link taken as equal, is a tiling of hyperbolic d-space by ideal simplices; so hyperbolic network geometry can be the outcome of combinatorial growth rather than its cause, though the curvature comes from the equal-length convention and not from the growth | Bianconi and Rahmede (2017), [LIT-867](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-867.md): the tree dual is immediate and the degree law (geometric for d + s = 1, γ = 2 + 1/(d + s − 1) for d + s > 1) is derived by a master equation; the hyperbolic geometry is a drawing, ideal simplices in the Poincaré ball, with uniqueness asserted. The source itself says unequal link lengths would fit the same complex in a sphere. It does not measure hyperbolicity on the graph, and it does not show real networks grow this way. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-242](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-242.md) | A spiral of silence can make a small, fixed minority opinion look far more widespread than it is without any member changing belief, and in the model that shows it the network's direct distortion of what members see is small | Vilone and Polizzi (2024), [LIT-939](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-939.md), read in full in [NOTE-810](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-810.md). In agent-based models on scale-free networks with fixed private beliefs, a hard-core minority drives 55–60% of agents, nearly all of them in the majority, into silence, so that expressed and perceived opinion lean far toward the minority. The friendship-paradox distortion is small and of no fixed sign. This is simulation only. Beliefs never change, so nothing here shows a community coming to believe the minority view, and the majority is overturned only when the minority exceeds about 30%. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-254](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-254.md) | Tangle-defined cohesion matches network communities only where community structure is strongly delineated, and tangles of one to three vertices recur beside the ones that do | Salter-Duke (2024), [LIT-955](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-955.md), a PhD thesis read in full in [NOTE-814](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-814.md). Edge-connectivity tangles, computed exactly at low order on eleven small real networks, give communities close to standard methods where structure is strong (yeast PPI) and none or almost none where it is weak (karate club, C. elegans, college football at the orders reached), and where tangles divide a network some hold only one to three vertices. The relation is read by eye from eight networks, and the vertex sets depend on the author's assignment rule. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-276](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-276.md) | In a network of identical units with identical couplings, the orbits of the graph's symmetry group are synchronization clusters, and a cluster moved only by its own factor of the group can lose synchrony while the others keep it | Pecora et al. (2014), [LIT-960](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-960.md), read in [NOTE-775](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-775.md): eq. (1), the IRR block-diagonalization (eqs. 2–4, 7), the derivation of isolated desynchronization (eq. 6) and an 11-node electro-optic experiment. The pattern of clusters that can synchronize is read from the wiring; whether each does is set by the dynamics through its own transverse block. Symmetry is sufficient, not necessary, for clusters. The paper says nothing about external drive, so the use of these clusters as a sign of coupling rather than a shared cue is the record's inference. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-321](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-321.md) | Under repeated DeGroot averaging, a large society's consensus converges to the truth if and only if the largest influence weight vanishes, so network structure alone, not the members' common updating rule, decides whether the group belief is right | Golub & Jackson (2010), [LIT-999](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-999.md), Proposition 2 with Lemma 1, Corollary 1, Proposition 3 and Theorem 1, read in [NOTE-840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-840.md) with the main proofs checked. The members are naïve, not sound: they ignore repeated information, and only the first round is Bayesian. The result is in a model with fixed weights, independent signals and n → ∞. Speed of consensus and its correctness are independent. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) | A stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, makes greedy search cost grow about logarithmically with the number of items on uniform random data in 4 and 8 dimensions, where single-layer navigable graphs grow polylogarithmically; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. They build an index like a skip list, with proximity graphs in place of linked lists, and argue that search costs a constant per layer over O(log N) layers. That holds if each layer is an exact Delaunay graph of bounded mean degree. HNSW does not build such graphs, and Delaunay degree grows exponentially with dimension. For the graphs it does build, logarithmic growth is measured on uniform random data at d = 4 and 8, and at d = 128 (200M SIFT) the growth departs from a logarithm. The paper gives no worst-case bound and no recall guarantee. Construction is argued to cost about N searches. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). Proved for the two-dimensional lattice: with nodes, local links and the number of long-range links fixed, changing only the exponent r of the long-range link distribution moves the expected delivery time of the best decentralized searcher from O((log n)²) at r = 2 to a power of n at every other r, including r = 0, where paths of polylogarithmic length exist. The upper bound is proved only for one local and one long-range link per node; the k-dimensional statement (r = k) is asserted, not proved; the family is inverse power laws of a distance every node can compute, so it does not show that no other link structure is navigable. | Active |
| [THEORY-385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-385.md) | In a proximity-graph index over data in isolated clusters, linking each new item to its nearest neighbours leaves greedy search stuck at cluster boundaries and short of high recall, while linking a candidate only when it is nearer the new item than to any neighbour already chosen keeps the clusters connected and search fast; on uniform or very high-dimensional data the two rules differ little, and the evidence is the authors' own tests on synthetic and benchmark data | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md). In HNSW, each new element's neighbours are chosen either as its M nearest candidates or by a pruning rule that keeps a candidate only if it is nearer the new element than to any neighbour already kept, a rule related to the relative neighbourhood graph. On 10M random d = 10 vectors in 100 isolated clusters, nearest-neighbour links failed to reach high recall and the pruning rule did not. In every test reported, the rule was at least as good. Its gain was largest at low dimension, at high recall, and on clustered data, and small on uniform or very high-dimensional data. These are the authors' benchmarks: one clustered dataset, synthetic, with no independent replication in this reading. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) | In hyperbolic graph embeddings trained on link-prediction or classification losses, distance from the origin is only a partial reading of hierarchical level: on synthetic trees the root is not innermost and level order is recovered for 69–75% of node pairs, and a loss built on pairwise distances leaves the origin arbitrary | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md). On two synthetic 3-ary trees of eight levels, HGCN leaves the root at hyperbolic distance 1.8–3.3 from the origin where the minimum is 1.2–2.4, the distances are roughly normal rather than leaf-heavy, and radius orders true levels for 69–75% of 5,000 random pairs. Recentring on the centroid plus an outward push raises that to 75–84%. The diagnosis rests on one architecture, two synthetic trees and one table without variance, and the paper does not separate a real failure to order levels from the origin's arbitrariness under losses that see only pairwise distances. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-422](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-422.md) | In the standard formal models of group learning, no communication network is best for every epistemic problem: costly transmission favours minimally connected or star networks, pooling of estimates by averaging favours regular networks, and learning by trying in bandit problems can favour sparse ones, so a group's network cannot be judged until its learning problem is known | Zollman (2013), [LIT-716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-716.md), a survey read in [NOTE-567](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-567.md). Each result it gathers is proved or simulated in its source (Bala and Goyal, Jackson and Wolinsky, DeGroot, Hegselmann and Krause, Zollman). Under their idealisations the optimal structure changes with the problem, so neither "too little communication" nor unequal centrality is by itself an epistemic pathology. It is a claim about models: utilitarian optimality only, with fairness, robustness and the route to the optimum left out. | Active |
| [THEORY-456](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-456.md) | Iterating Ollivier–Ricci flow on edge weights lengthens edges between communities relative to edges within them, so a weight threshold can separate the communities; but the separation is proved only on symmetric clique graphs under the uniform neighbour measure, and there only by a constant factor for gateway edges, and on a two-block stochastic block model the method fails at an inter/intra ratio near 0.55, where other methods still recover the blocks and well short of the detectability threshold near 0.78 | Ni, Lin, Luo & Gao (2019), [LIT-004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-004.md), read in full with its SI in [NOTE-006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-006.md), which checked Lemma E.1 by linear programming and iterated the proof's matrix. The flow w ← (1 − κ)d replaces each weight by the transport cost between the endpoints' neighbourhoods; bridge edges, with few shared neighbours, are negatively curved and grow. Theorem 4.1 (α = p = 0, cliques G(a,b), a > b ≥ 2) shows only non-gateway intra-clique edges shrinking; gateway edges grow at the inter-community rate with a ratio k ∈ (0,1) from Maple. Experiments use α = ½, p = 2, which no theorem covers. The Kesten–Stigum figure is [NOTE-006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-006.md)'s calculation. | Active |
| [THEORY-502](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-502.md) | Forman–Ricci curvature of a graph edge, taken with no cells above the edges, depends only on the weights of the edge, its two endpoints and the edges adjacent to it, and with unit weights reduces to 4 − deg(v₁) − deg(v₂); it is a local, closed-form degree-and-weight statistic that sees no triangles or cycles, unlike Ollivier's curvature, which needs a transport problem per edge | Weber, Saucan & Jost (2016; J. The formula (Eq. 11) is Forman's (2003) Bochner–Weitzenböck curvature specialised to a 1-dimensional complex by dropping the parent terms; the unit-weight form is [NOTE-026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-026.md)'s substitution, not stated in the paper. The paper's applications (an EMD distance between curvature distributions, a Ricci flow for change detection, a Laplacian flow for denoising) are one-table or one-figure demonstrations, and several of its formulas carry sign and consistency slips, so it is cited here for the definition only. | Active |
| [THEORY-576](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-576.md) | In a bundled network, one fiber graph attached at a single node to every node of a base graph, the low Laplacian spectrum is the base spectrum divided by the fiber size to first order, so the gap exponent (Fiedler dimension) is set by the base while the density-of-states exponent (spectral dimension) is the fiber's; the two come apart generically and coincide only in special cases, and relaxation then decays with the spectral dimension at intermediate times but equilibrates on a time set by the Fiedler dimension | Grimaldi, Villegas, Vezzani, Burioni, Cassi & Gabrielli (2025; PRE Letter 2026), [LIT-028](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-028.md), read in full with its SM in [NOTE-005](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-005.md), which re-derived the key steps and checked them numerically on the comb. λ_{n1} = ℓ^b_{n1}/N_f gives d_g = 2(d_f,f + d_f,b)/(d_f,f + 2d_f,b/d_g,b) in the base-controlled regime; d_s = d_s,f is earlier work by the same group. The comb has d_s = 1 and d_g = 4/3. Proved for one graph class only; the paper's composite finite-size scaling prefactors (SM Eqs. 25, 29) are wrong, and its "generic property of composite architectures" outruns the proof. | Active |
| [THEORY-598](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-598.md) | Group interactions that enter a dynamical model linearly, as in diffusion on simplices or random walks on hypergraphs with edge-independent vertex weights, reduce to pairwise dynamics on a reweighted graph; the abrupt transitions, bistability and stabilised coexistence reported for higher-order systems come from group terms that enter nonlinearly, and whether the representation is a hypergraph or a simplicial complex is itself a modelling claim that changes the outcome | Battiston et al. (2020), [LIT-091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-091.md), read in full in [NOTE-057](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-057.md). A review: the reduction results are its own §V algebra (three-body linear diffusion becomes a weighted graph Laplacian, Eq. 35) and reported results it cites (Chitra and Raphael on hypergraph walks); the nonlinear effects are one-paper summaries, mostly mean-field or all-to-all. The review never states the condition as a result, and its introduction and conclusion claim more ("no doubts", "profoundly change"), citing linear cases among the examples. The condition is the record's reading of what its body shows; edge-dependent vertex weights also escape the reduction. | Active |
| [THEORY-649](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-649.md) | When agents holding uniformly random consistent theories over two or three atomic sentences each average their theories once, bit by bit, with all peers within a Hamming bound of confidence, an individual agent ends up with the inconsistent theory at most 1.81% of the time, but the chance that some agent in the group does reaches 6.4% for two sentences and 16.9% for three | Wenmackers (2011), [LIT-163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-163.md), chapter 5, read in [NOTE-139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-139.md). | [THEORY-659](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-659.md) | In the EEAS's 2024 sample of 505 foreign information manipulation incidents, the overt state voice is a small core: of the 2,055 channels that recur across incidents, 20% are attributed to Russia, 3.5% to China and 76.5% are not attributed, after some 28,000 disposable inauthentic accounts are set aside; the sample is not representative, and the four-tier Exposure Matrix used to grade channels' ties to a state is unvalidated | European External Action Service (2025), [LIT-084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-084.md), the 3rd EEAS report on FIMI threats, read in [NOTE-060](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-060.md). | [THEORY-660](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-660.md) | The local branching geometry of physical tree networks, neurons, blood vessels, trees, corals and plants, is set by minimising the surface area of tubes that must keep a minimum circumference, not by minimising length: this predicts trifurcations once links are thick relative to their separation (χ = w/r above about 0.83) and orthogonal sprouts once one branch is much thinner than the other two (ρ = w′/w below about 0.6), both departures from Steiner trees that the data show qualitatively | Meng, Piazza, Both, Barzel & Barabási (2026), [LIT-069](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-069.md), read in full with the SI in [NOTE-075](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-075.md). The random-terminal prediction is a sigmoid fitted to one tetrahedron, trifurcations are partly made by a merging rule, the one robustness check moves the key statistic 4.3-fold, and the sprouting breakpoints are chosen per dataset with no null. Real motifs are about 25% longer than Steiner, which the model leaves unexplained. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-675](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-675.md) | Without a shared stable start, the linear barrier between solutions of one objective depends on the structure of the training data: between GCNs it falls with graph density and feature separability and is highest at middling homophily, and between federated-averaging models it grows with client heterogeneity and falls with width | Li et al.
